Talked to one at a time, each investor holds a free option and waits; and the first commitment is the hard one — "Once you start getting investors to commit, it becomes increasingly easy to get more to." - [#] Investor silence means different things at different stages. Before a first meeting it is the default; after a first call that named no next step it is usually a soft no; more than a week after a partners' meeting it is usually a no; in diligence it is the work; after a term sheet it is paperwork, until the timetable slips. pb:founder_office.heu.investor_relations: - [#] Most passes are decisions about timing, stage or a metric, and each of those carries an implicit date on which it stops being true. Record the date, not the refusal. Only thesis and team passes are verdicts. — why: A fund passing on stage is saying its cheque does not fit today's round, which changes at the next round without anyone changing their mind; a fund passing on timing is reading its own cycle. Both are scheduling facts wearing the vocabulary of rejection, and the vocabulary is what gets recorded. Investors who reject a company "are some of your warmest leads for future fundraising" — any who "spent significant time deciding probably came close to saying yes" (Graham). Thesis and team are different in kind: judgments about what the company is, which no date changes. (not yet reviewed)
- [#] Reopen after a pass: Read the passing message for its reason: stage, timing, traction, thesis, team, or none given. Only the first three reopen. Thesis and team do not reopen for this company, and pretending otherwise costs the relationship as well as the time.; Capture the exact words — "come back when you have a lead", "we look again above fifty thousand a month in revenue". Paraphrase loses the threshold, and the threshold is the asset. Where none was given, record that rather than inventing one.; Thank them, confirm the condition back in their own words, and ask for nothing. Arguing with a pass turns a warm future conversation into a closed one, and this is the moment the temptation is strongest.; A date where the condition is a date; a watch on the metric where it is a threshold. An unscheduled intention to follow up later is indistinguishable from having dropped it.; Open on what changed against their stated condition and nothing else. "You said come back with a lead; we have one" is a new conversation. "Just checking in" is the one they already declined, and it teaches them to skim the next. — success: The re-approach produces a meeting, or a reply that reopens the conversation. — wait 30 days (not yet reviewed)

- [#] The conditional deferral: Take the conversation out of the round's count. "Send me updates" commits nobody, and "I want to invest in you, but I don't lead" translates to "No, except yes if you turn out to be a hot deal" (Graham).; Record exactly what would bring them back — a lead, a revenue figure, a launch — in their words. "Keep me posted" with nothing named is recorded as no condition, never filled in with a plausible one.; Thank them, confirm the condition back in their words, and say they will hear when it changes. Arguing with a deferral turns a door left open into a closed one.; Add them to the update list: growth, cash and burn, what the company needs, sent every month — the cadence Aaron Harris, a former Y Combinator partner, recommends. Each update is a dated reading of progress against their condition.; When the condition is met, write to them about that and nothing else — "You said come back with a lead; we have one." A check-in is the conversation they already deferred.; If the updates in the window draw no reply and no question, stop expecting them to reopen the conversation by themselves. pb:founder_office.heu.investor_relations: - [#] When the turn is ours, the clock is running against us and nobody will say so. Age the conversations where we owe the reply before the ones where they do. — why: A fund sees far more companies than it can fund — one partner described 500 to 800 plans a year for one or two deals done (David Hornik, quoted by Paul Graham) — and loses nothing by dropping one. A partial reply left unanswered reads to it as a company that lost momentum, the one attribute a raise cannot afford to project. The asymmetry is structural: our silence is informative to them; theirs, before the stage says otherwise, is not informative to us. (not yet reviewed)

- [#] A round's momentum comes from investors seeing other investors move. Run every conversation in parallel, and let each live investor hear real progress elsewhere; a conversation run on its own has no clock. — why: "The biggest factor in most investors' opinions of you is the opinion of other investors" (Graham, "How to Raise Money"), and getting far along with one firm "will sometimes provoke other firms, even good ones, to make up their minds, lest they lose the deal" ("Investor Herd Dynamics"). Talked to one at a time, each investor holds a free option and waits; and the first commitment is the hard one — "Once you start getting investors to commit, it becomes increasingly easy to get more to." (not yet reviewed)

- [#] Count an investor in only when they have made a definite offer — an amount and a valuation or cap, with no conditions — and confirmed it in writing. Until then, treat them as a no, however warm they sound. — why: "Investors habitually seem more positive than they are", and some "use language that makes it sound as if they're committing, but which doesn't actually commit them" (Graham). "We'd love to be part of this", "we're in if you find a lead" and "we can do fifty to a hundred and fifty" are not offers: Y Combinator's Handshake Deal Protocol defines an offer as an amount plus a valuation or cap and refuses ranges and conditions, because a founder who keeps room for a conditional yes is the only party it binds. (not yet reviewed)

- [#] Investor silence means different things at different stages. Before a first meeting it is the default; after a first call that named no next step it is usually a soft no; more than a week after a partners' meeting it is usually a no; in diligence it is the work; after a term sheet it is paperwork, until the timetable slips. Read silence by the stage, never by its length alone. — why: Each stage has a different decider and a different clock. A firm in diligence is calling references and writing its memo (Gompers et al. measured ten reference calls on average); a partnership decides in a weekly meeting, and its rejection "will rarely come in the form of an actual 'no'" (Dixon); and investors at every stage prefer an open option to a closed door — "Some of the worse ones never actually do say no; they just stop replying to your emails" (Graham). The same twelve days of quiet is therefore nothing in diligence and an answer after a partners' meeting. (not yet reviewed)
